title: Building Reusable Component Architecture in React
excerpt: How I structure component folders, props, and variants so a design system stays consistent as a product grows past a dozen screens.
content: Most React codebases don't fail because of a bad framework choice — they fail because components grow one prop at a time until nobody can predict what a change will break.
The pattern I default to: a small set of primitive, style-only components (Button, Card, Badge) composed into feature components that own behavior and data, never the other way around.

Variants live behind a single `variant` prop backed by class-variance-authority, not a spread of boolean props like `isPrimary`, `isLarge`, `isRounded`. It keeps the API surface predictable and the Tailwind classes centralized in one place.
The payoff shows up months later: a rebrand or design tweak touches a handful of primitive files instead of every screen in the app.

title: Zustand vs. Redux: Choosing State Management by Problem Shape
excerpt: After shipping both in production, here's the practical difference I actually care about — not the philosophy debate.
content: Redux earns its ceremony when state is genuinely shared across unrelated feature areas and you need time-travel debugging or middleware-driven side effects.
Zustand wins when state is scoped to a feature — a booking calendar, a multi-step form — and you want to avoid boilerplate without losing devtools support.

On the Co-Workspace Management project, booking/resource availability lived in a normalized Zustand store per location; cross-cutting auth and notification state stayed in Redux from an earlier module.
The real lesson: pick per problem, not per project. Mixing both is fine if the boundaries are clear.

title: Animation That Clarifies State, Not Just Decorates It
excerpt: A framework for deciding when motion earns its place in a UI, and when it's just noise.
content: Before adding a transition, I ask what state change it's communicating — loading, success, focus, hierarchy. If the answer is 'it looks nice,' that's a signal to cut it or shorten it.

Framer Motion's `whileInView` and layout animations do most of the heavy lifting for reveal and reordering. GSAP earns its keep only for scroll-pinned or timeline-scrubbed sequences that Framer can't express cleanly.
Every animation in this portfolio respects `prefers-reduced-motion` — accessibility isn't optional polish, it's part of the animation spec from day one.

title: Setting Performance Budgets Your Team Will Actually Keep
excerpt: Lighthouse scores are easy to chase and easy to lose. Here's how to make performance a release gate instead of a one-time audit.
content: A performance budget only works if it's enforced automatically — bundle-size checks in CI catch regressions long before a manual Lighthouse run would.
Dynamic imports for below-the-fold, interaction-heavy sections (carousels, modals, charts) consistently gave the biggest wins with the least risk.
The hardest part isn't the tooling, it's the review culture: treating a bundle-size increase the same way you'd treat a failing test.
